clue.text: Desert ship commanded by him

parts.note: the ship of the desert is the camel, and the man who 'commands' it is its driver

explanation.surface: A riddle about the captain of a sandbound vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ship of the desert' is a stock name for the camel, so its commander is a camel driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A camel driver is the person who leads and controls the animal, as a captain commands a ship.

clue.text: Ape with another animal — not the original sort

parts.note: to ape is to copy or imitate
a cat is an animal besides the ape

explanation.surface: An ape together with some other creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ape' looks like a noun naming an animal, which 'another animal' seems to confirm; it is the verb meaning imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: An imitator copies others instead of being an original.

clue.text: Did it register plus 70 at Babylon?

definitions.text: Did it register plus 70 at Babylon?

parts.words: Did it register plus 70 at Babylon?
parts.note: the nursery rhyme asks how many miles to Babylon, answering three score and ten, so the mileage gauge would have clocked seventy

explanation.surface: A question about whether something recorded over seventy in ancient Mesopotamia.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'How many miles to Babylon? Three score and ten' supplies the 70; the device that counts miles travelled would show it.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's distance gauge records miles driven, as an odometer does.

clue.text: A non-metaphorical misprint

explanation.surface: A plain-spoken typing error.
explanation.walkthrough: In printing, a misprinted letter has long been called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken word for word rather than figuratively; and a printer's term for a typographical error.

clue.text: Creator of Enigma variations in Germany

definitions.text: Creator of Enigma variations in Germany

parts.words: Creator of Enigma variations in Germany
parts.note: Enigma was the German wartime cipher machine, so its varied scrambled messages were made by someone putting them into code

explanation.surface: Points towards Elgar, composer of the Enigma Variations, wrongly placed in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Elgar's orchestral Enigma Variations; the clue means the German Enigma cipher machine and the person turning messages into cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who turns plain text into cipher produces scrambled versions of messages.

clue.text: Small contribution to degree — not the best

explanation.surface: A modest part in earning a university degree, falling short of first place.
explanation.walkthrough: A degree of arc divides into sixty minutes and each minute into sixty smaller units; also, the runner-up finishes behind the best.
explanation.definitionFit: One sixtieth of a minute of arc is a tiny part of an angular degree; the runner-up position comes just after first.

clue.text: Rock sound produced, by George!

parts.note: George Sand was the French novelist, and the possessive George Sand's gives the S
a tone is a musical sound

explanation.surface: An exclamation, 'by George!', about some noise made by a rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by George!' looks like an oath; it means the sound (TONE) is George Sand's, the French woman writer who used that pen name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a sedimentary stone formed of compressed grains.

clue.text: Dismiss till manager appears

explanation.surface: A shop manager sacks the person in charge of the cash register.
explanation.walkthrough: To cashier someone is to dismiss them from service, especially in the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Discharge in disgrace from service; and the employee who handles money at a cash register.

clue.text: Two sorts of present out of place?

parts.note: present in time is now
present in space is here

explanation.surface: Two gifts that are misplaced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' looks like a gift; it means present in time and present in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Nowhere means in no location at all, so not in any place.

clue.text: Queen's enemy we wish to see confounded

definitions.text: Queen's enemy we wish to see confounded

parts.words: Queen's enemy we wish to see confounded
parts.note: recalls the British national anthem's verse asking God to 'confound their politics', meaning the politics of the monarch's enemies

explanation.surface: A loyal subject hoping a royal foe is thwarted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God Save the Queen' has the line 'Confound their politics', so the person whose politics are confounded is cast as the enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: A party statesman practises politics, the very thing the anthem asks to be confounded.

clue.text: Points on compass connected by needle

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for the compass point south
E is the abbreviation for the compass point east
W is the abbreviation for the compass point west
N is the abbreviation for the compass point north

explanation.surface: Directions on a compass linked by its magnetic needle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface needle is a compass needle; in the definition it is a sewing needle.
explanation.definitionFit: Stitched together means joined with thread drawn through by a needle.

clue.text: County village of fiction with riches distributed about

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go round the fictional village's name
the letters of riches are spread around in a new order

parts.note: Ambridge is the imaginary village in the long-running BBC radio soap The Archers

explanation.surface: A rural setting from a novel scattered with wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distributed' rearranges RICHES into C...SHIRE, and 'about' wraps those letters around AMBRIDGE, the village of The Archers, a British radio soap.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an English shire, an administrative county in East Anglia.

clue.text: Steele's publication disheartens this gossip

parts.note: Richard Steele's periodical The Tatler is what you get by taking the heart (middle letter) out of the word we want

explanation.surface: An eighteenth-century journal outdoes a chatterbox in gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: remove the central T from the seven-letter answer and you get TATLER, the journal Steele founded in 1709.
explanation.definitionFit: A telltale or chatterer spreads rumours, which is what a gossip does.

clue.text: Cut is altogether under this

parts.note: a cut goes through the outer layer of skin, and being 'in the altogether' means wearing nothing but skin

explanation.surface: Something beneath which a wound lies entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altogether' hints at the British idiom 'in the altogether', meaning naked.
explanation.definitionFit: The outermost layer of skin is the surface a cut breaks through.

clue.text: Artist has to live in royal residence

indicators.note: the word for living sits inside the royal residence

parts.note: a court is the household and residence of a monarch
to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: A painter is lodging at the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Gustave Courbet was the nineteenth-century French Realist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Courbet was a French painter, a leader of the Realist movement.

clue.text: Cheat in game of chance caught by brother officer

indicators.note: the cheating phrase is held between the letters for brother

parts.note: to rig a die is to cheat when throwing dice

explanation.surface: A cheat at gambling is nabbed by a sibling who is an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught by' places RIG A DIE inside B...R.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigadier is a senior army officer commanding a brigade.

clue.text: Am I partly splitting nail in four for local girl?

indicators.note: the three letters of Am I are split up and slipped one by one between the letters of the nail

parts.note: a four-letter nail is a brad; its first letter here
the first of the letters of the words Am I
the second letter of brad, the four-letter nail
the second of the letters of the words Am I
the third letter of brad, the four-letter nail
the third of the letters of the words Am I
the last letter of brad, the four-letter nail

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they are a nail-splitting pub worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly splitting' means A, M and I go one at a time into the gaps of BRAD, a small nail with four letters, giving B-A-R-M-A-I-D. A local is a British pub, so a local girl serves behind its bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman serving drinks at the pub, which British speakers call the local.

clue.text: Judge takes part in rare reform

indicators.note: the piece goes inside the rearranged word
the word rare is reshaped into a new arrangement

parts.note: a bit is a part or piece

explanation.surface: An umpire involves himself in an unusual reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' rearranges RARE as ARER, and 'in' puts BIT inside to give AR-BIT-ER.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbiter decides disputes, as a judge does.

clue.text: Prosper at French court as writer

parts.note: the forename Prosper and a place at the court of Napoleon III point to the author of Carmen

explanation.surface: Someone thriving at a French royal court as an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prosper' looks like a verb meaning thrive; it is the forename of the French writer who was a favourite at the court of Napoleon III and Empress Eugenie.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosper Merimee was a French novelist, author of Carmen.

clue.text: Sense of significance

explanation.surface: A phrase asking how important something feels.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the import of a word and its purpose or significance are its sense; 'of' joins two synonyms.

clue.text: Employ a different sort of staff for holiday

indicators.note: the letters of the preceding words are turned into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Hiring a new kind of workers for the festive season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees; it is a pole, set up for May Day dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall decorated pole erected for May Day celebrations.

clue.text: Clears account, having settled what was owing

parts.note: two people who are quits have paid off their debts to each other

explanation.surface: Settling a bank account once all debts are paid.
explanation.definitionFit: To find someone not guilty frees them of a charge.

clue.text: How American supposed visitor might sound

indicators.note: the answer is said like the word for a visitor

parts.note: a guest is a visitor

explanation.surface: Asking how an American guest would pronounce something.
explanation.walkthrough: Americans say 'I guess' where Britons say 'I suppose'.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage to guess is to think or reckon something likely.

clue.text: London area for philosopher, by no means trendy

parts.note: George Berkeley was an Irish idealist philosopher
someone square is old-fashioned and conventional

explanation.surface: A thinker who is decidedly uncool is given a part of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkeley Square is a garden square in Mayfair, London.
explanation.definitionFit: This square in Mayfair is a well-known place in the British capital.

clue.text: Check part of system's temperature twice

indicators.note: the answer is a piece taken from inside the following words

explanation.surface: Checking a section of a system's temperature reading two times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' because the run appears both in 'sySTEMs' and across 'syStem'S TEMperature'.
explanation.definitionFit: To stem a flow is to check or stop it.

clue.text: Party types hope theirs won't go with a swing

definitions.text: Party types hope theirs won't go with a swing

parts.words: Party types hope theirs won't go with a swing
parts.note: a party here is a political party, and an electoral swing could wipe out its winning margin

explanation.surface: Revellers hoping their celebration will not flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' and 'go with a swing' suggest a lively social gathering; in elections a swing of votes is what threatens a party's lead.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning margins of votes or seats are what politicians fear losing to an electoral swing.

clue.text: Parts of course

parts.note: a golf course has putting areas, and a meal course may include leafy vegetables

explanation.surface: Sections of a course.
explanation.walkthrough: The course is a golf course, whose closely mown putting areas are named for their colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The putting surfaces on a golf links are sections of the playing ground.

clue.text: Cut with a 3 and tore off a strip

indicators.note: 3 down is a misprint, so one letter of the word for cut is printed wrongly

parts.note: material that is censored has had parts cut out

explanation.surface: Edited with a typo and then a scolding.
explanation.walkthrough: The 3 is 3 down, a printer's literal: one letter of CENSORED is misprinted, O becoming U. To tear someone off a strip is British slang for scolding them.
explanation.definitionFit: Reprimanded severely, which is what the British idiom of tearing a strip off someone means.
